title: Metal-organic framework-confined Co_3O_4 for humidity-immune ozone decomposition

paper_content.abstract:
Ground-level ozone (O ) is a major air pollutant, and catalytic decomposition represents a
3
promising strategy for its removal. However, maintaining high catalytic efficiency under humid
conditions remains a considerable challenge. In this study, we encapsulate ultrafine metal oxides
(UMOs; e.g., Co O , NiO) within the nanopores of an Fe O-cluster-based metal–organic
3 4 3
framework, PCN-333(Fe), for catalytic O decomposition. The optimized 30% Co O @PCN-
3 3 4
333(Fe) catalyst achieves sustained 100% O conversion for over 120 hours in a continuous airflow
3
containing 40 ppm O under high space velocity (1.75 × 105 Sh-1) and a broad range of humidity
3
(10-90% RH). Mechanistic investigations reveal that the exceptional performance originates from
an interfacial hydrogen-atom transfer process between Co O and the Fe O clusters of PCN-
3 4 3
333(Fe), as confirmed by in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier-transform spectroscopy
(DRIFTS) and in situ Raman spectroscopy. This work proposes a general principle for designing
humidity-immune catalytic interfaces between metal oxides and porous materials, thereby
providing a practical foundation for sustainable control of pollutant emissions in complex
environments.
paper_content.introduction:
Ground-level ozone (O ) has emerged as a major global air pollutant, posing serious threats to both
3
environmental quality and public health1, 2. Outdoor O is primarily generated through
3
photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds under sunlight,
while indoor O may accumulate from emissions produced by photocopiers, laser printers,
3
ultraviolet lamps, and disinfection devices3, 4. As a potent oxidant, O remains relatively stable at
3
typical ambient concentrations (ppb level)5; however, long-term exposure has been associated with
respiratory disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and even premature mortality6, 7. The World Health
Organization has recommended that the 8-h average O concentration exceeding 100 μg m-3 (≈ 51
3
ppb) poses health risks8. Alarmingly, O levels exceeding 150 ppb are frequently reported in many
3
regions, reflecting severe pollution episodes. These observations underscore the urgent need for
efficient, durable, and environmentally sustainable strategies for O removal.
3
Among various control measures, catalytic decomposition is regarded as the most promising
strategy owing to its high efficiency and absence of harmful by-products9, 10. Conventional
transition-metal oxides exhibit notable activity but suffer from rapid deactivation under humid
conditions, where water molecules compete strongly for active sites11-13. Dispersing ultrafine metal
oxides (UMOs) on carbonaceous or porous substrates can partially alleviate these issues14, yet such
systems still face challenges of weak host–guest interfacial coupling, limited control over particle
size, and heterogeneous distributions of active sites. In contrast, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)
offer distinct advantages, including tunable organic linkers to balance
hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, robust inorganic nodes to act as active sites, and hierarchical
porosity to facilitate mass transport15-19. Nevertheless, most reported UMO-MOF composites rely
on external loading, which often leads to non-uniform particle distributions, pore blockage, and
reduced accessibility of active sites20-22. Therefore, designing UMO-MOF catalysts with well-
defined structures, strong interfacial interactions, and high stability is of paramount importance,
offering new opportunities to overcome current limitations and realize highly efficient O
3
catalytic
decomposition.
Herein, we report a series of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) composites (UMOs = ultrafine Co O or
3 4
NiO nanoparticles), in which the oxide nanoparticles are precisely encapsulated inside the
nanopores of PCN-333(Fe) rather than simply deposited on the external surface. Among them, 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) achieves 100% O conversion across a wide humidity (10-90% RH) at room
3 4 3
temperature, and maintains long-term stability for over 120 h. DFT calculations combined with in
situ spectroscopy reveal that the exceptional catalytic performance originates from interfacial
hydrogen-atom transfer between Co O and Fe O clusters of PCN-333(Fe), which facilitates
3 4 3
stepwise O activation, improves O release efficiency, and accelerates active-site regeneration.
3 2
Furthermore, the remarkable humidity immunity arises from the MOF-confined protection of
active sites from water invasion, while water molecules actively participate in the reaction pathway
rather than competing with O . This work establishes a fundamental principle for engineering
3
interfacial hydrogen-atom transfer within MOF-confined oxide catalysts, thereby providing a
practical foundation for achieving sustainable pollutant control under complex and variable
environmental conditions.
paper_content.results:
Syntheses and Structural Characterization of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe)
The synthetic route of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) is depicted in Fig. 1. A sonication-microwave
confinement strategy was developed to achieve the precise incorporation of ultrafine metal oxide
nanoparticles within the nanopores of PCN-333(Fe). Initially, activated PCN-333(Fe) was
dispersed homogeneously in a hydrophobic solvent (e.g. n-hexane) by ultrasonication, preventing
aggregation and exposing the hierarchical pore system. Subsequently, controlled amounts of
UMOs precursors were introduced under 0°C, enabling their gradual penetration into the
nanopores of framework. After an aging process that facilitated precursor anchoring, the mixture
was carefully filtered and underwent microwave treatment, which induced rapid in situ nucleation
and growth of UMOs as highly dispersed clusters confined within the pores of PCN-333(Fe). This
step ensured both uniform nanoparticle distribution and preservation of the host crystallinity.
Finally, careful purification removed residual reactants without damaging the porous architecture.
This synthetic strategy thus provides a versatile platform for embedding nanoscale metal oxides
into MOFs, achieving strong interfacial coupling and well-defined hybrid architectures for
catalytic applications.
To elucidate the structural characteristics of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe), we selected 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) as a representative material. The MTN-type zeolitic topology of PCN-333
3 4
(Fig. 1) consists of a dual-mesopore network formed by supertetrahedral building units, with two
types of mesocages (4.2 and 5.5 nm in diameter) interconnected by pore windows of ∼2.6 and 3.0
nm, thereby providing spatially well-defined compartments for nanoparticle encapsulation23, 24.
Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy
(AC-HAADF-STEM) was employed to probe the structural integrity and encapsulation behavior25.
The pristine PCN-333(Fe) framework displays periodically arranged mesopores on the (110) plane
(Fig. 2a). Upon encapsulation, the 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) sample preserves the parent pore
3 4
periodicity (Fig. 2b), yet exhibits locally elevated contrast, directly evidencing pore occupation by
Co O nanoparticles (Fig. 2c). EDS elemental mapping further confirms homogeneous Co
3 4
distribution across single MOF crystals (Fig. S1). The encapsulated Co O nanoparticles exhibit a
3 4
uniform size of 3.4-3.9 nm (average 3.6 ± 0.1 nm, Fig. S2), which matches the mesoporous cavity
dimensions of PCN-333. Scanning Electron Microscope reveals well-retained octahedral
morphology with smooth surfaces and absence of surface-deposited aggregates (Fig. S3),
corroborating true intracrystalline encapsulation. These observations unambiguously confirm that
Co O nanoparticles are formed in situ and precisely confined within the nanopores of PCN-
3 4
333(Fe), without compromising the structural integrity of its framework.
To probe the chemical state of Co element in 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe), Co K-edge X-ray
3 4
absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS)
spectroscopy were performed, revealing an absorption edge between Co foil and bulk Co O ,
3 4
closer to Co O , indicating a slightly reduced oxidation state due to nanoconfinement-induced
3 4
interface effects (Fig. 3a)26. Fourier-transformed EXAFS (FT-EXAFS, Fig. 3b) reveals a
prominent Co-O coordination at ~1.42 Å, marginally shorter than the 1.46 Å path in bulk Co O 27,
3 4
28, while subsequent Co-Co coordination shells are markedly attenuated, directly evidencing the
highly dispersed and size-confined nature of the encapsulated clusters. Quantitative EXAFS fitting
using crystallographic Co O parameters yields excellent agreement (Fig. 3c), unequivocally
3 4
confirming Co O as the dominant crystalline phase while exhibiting subtle oxidation state
3 4
reduction associated with elevated oxygen vacancy concentrations.
Powder XRD patterns, photograph, and FT-IR spectra (Fig. 3d and Figs. S4-S5) confirm the
preservation of PCN-333(Fe)'s crystalline integrity following Co O incorporation across various
3 4
loadings. The absence of distinct Co O diffraction peaks precludes large particle formation,
3 4
instead indicating highly dispersed, ultra-small Co O nanoclusters29, 30. Raman spectroscopy
3 4
identifies the characteristic Co O peak at 682 cm-1 (Fig. 3e), confirming the encapsulated phase’s
3 4
identity as Co O 31, 32. N adsorption isotherms (Fig. 3f) and pore size analysis (Fig. S6) reveal a
3 4 2
systematic decrease in uptake capacity with increasing Co O loading, consistent with progressive
3 4
pore filling. Notably, unlike previous reports where metal oxides (e.g., TiO ) were confined solely
2
to mesopores, Co O in this work also occupies micropores (∼11 Å diameter), attributable to the
3 4
smaller size of its precursors25. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-
OES) quantitatively verifies Co O mass percentages of 9.4%, 18.6%, and 27.3% (Table S1),
3 4
aligning with the designated loadings. Similarly, structure characterization of NiO (Figs. S7-S10)
confirms its successful encapsulation within the PCN-333(Fe) framework.
O catalytic decomposition on UMOs@PCN-333(Fe)
3
The O catalytic decomposition performance of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) was evaluated with a
3
dynamic test at various humidity and temperature on a custom-built ozone analyzer at an inlet O
3
concentration of 40 ppm (Fig. S11). The effect of varying oxide loadings on catalyst under low
(10% RH) and high humidity (90% RH) conditions was first optimized (Figs. S12-S13).
Remarkably, 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) maintains complete O conversion for more than 160 h
3 4 3
at 40°C even under 10% RH (Fig. 4a), attesting to its outstanding durability in dry environments,
with a performance level comparable to the best catalysts reported to date13, 33-36. In addition, the
catalytic rate of O₃ decomposition over 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) was calculated to be 1.9
3 4
mmol·h-1·g -1. While performance exhibits humidity dependence, degrading to 120 hours at 90%
cat.
RH, this still represents exceptional longevity under high moisture stress compared to benchmark
materials. Furthermore, a pronounced positive temperature dependence of catalytic stability at
fixed low humidity (10% RH): 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) sustains 100% O conversion for 50
3 4 3
hours even at a low temperature of 10°C, underscoring its exceptional intrinsic activity and
robustness in O catalytic decomposition (Fig. 4b). Under 10% RH (Fig. 4c), the O conversion of
3 3
bulk Co O and pristine PCN-333(Fe) rapidly deactivate, reaching peak conversions of <10% and
3 4
<30% within 3 h, far below the sustained 100% activity of the composite. Even at 90% RH, 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) preserves its pronounced advantage, underscoring its superior humidity
3 4
immunity (Fig. 4d). These results highlight the synergistic catalysis arising from the MOF-
encapsulated UMOs structure.
The robustness of 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) to dynamic environmental fluctuations is shown
3 4
in Figs 4e-f. When subjected to fluctuating humidity cycles between 30% and 90% RH, or
temperature shifts between 10°C and 40°C, the material consistently maintains 100% O
3
conversion for 50+ hours without performance decay. This robust adaptability underscores its
capability to handle real-world atmospheric variability where humidity and temperature rarely
remain static. Optimization of the active phase loading is critical for maximizing humidity
immunity. Fig. 4g demonstrates that Co O @PCN-333(Fe) with 10% loading sustains 100%
3 4
conversion for only 20 hours at 90% RH, whereas increasing the loading to 30% extends this
duration to more than 160 hours. This pronounced Co O loading dependence unequivocally
3 4
demonstrates that achieving an optimal Co O density within the PCN-333(Fe) framework is
3 4
indispensable for preserving abundant and accessible catalytic sites, particularly under wet
environments.
Critically, 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) exhibits industry-relevant performance even under
3 4
simulated extreme environments, underscoring its substantial potential for practical application.
Challenging summertime conditions representative of the Yangtze River Delta region in China,
where intense photochemical activity and high humidity converge to produce severe O pollution
3
episodes, thereby underscoring the urgent necessity of effective removal strategies. Remarkably,
under these accelerated degradation conditions, 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) sustains complete O
3 4 3
decomposition for 120 hours (Fig. 4h). This superior stability highlights not only the high intrinsic
activity of the encapsulated architecture but also its resilience against the simultaneous thermal
and humidity stresses that typically deactivate conventional catalysts. Beyond the single Co O
3 4
system, the encapsulation strategy proves broadly generalizable for enhancing the catalytic
efficiency of diverse transition metal oxides. As demonstrated in Fig. 4i, PCN-333(Fe)
incorporating NiO, or Co O nanoclusters achieves over 120 hours of continuous and complete O
3 4 3
conversion under optimized conditions, markedly outperforming state-of-the-art benchmarks
(Table S2). Furthermore, systematic evaluations of NiO@PCN-333(Fe) (Figs. S14-S16) confirm
its outstanding decomposition activity across a wide range of environmental conditions. Although
all encapsulated composites deliver transformative stability enhancements relative to their bulk
oxide counterparts, 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) consistently demonstrates the highest activity-to-
3 4
stability balance, firmly establishing it as a leading candidate for scalable and durable industrial
O removal.
3
O Conversion Mechanism over 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe)
3 3 4
To elucidate the underlying mechanisms contributing to the excellent O catalytic
3
decomposition performance of 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
3 4
(XPS), in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy and in situ Raman
spectroscopy was performed. The chemical states of both Fe and Co underwent significant changes
after the encapsulation of Co O particles within the PCN-333(Fe) cages (Fig. 5a-b). Upon Co O
3 4 3 4
encapsulation, the Fe2+ content on PCN-333(Fe) increases from 45.1% to 61.9%, while the Co2+
content of Co O rises from 45.7% to 63.4%. Such concurrent enrichment of reduced Fe and Co
3 4
species underscores the emergence of an interfacial MOF-UMOs synergistic site, which is directly
promoted by the confined architecture. During O decomposition, oxygen vacancies are generated
3
to maintain electrostatic balance, and substantial evidence suggests that these vacancies act as the
dominant active sites, accounting for the high catalytic efficiency12, 37, 38. This conclusion is
corroborated by differential charge density calculation (Fig. S17), which reveals pronounced
charge transfer from MOF ligands to Fe and Co centers.
Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) analysis reveals that O exposure induces O •- species
3 2
in 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) when trapped by DMPO (Fig. S18). The in situ DRIFT spectrum
3 4
(Fig. 5c) exhibited prominent absorption bands at approximately 3660, 2125, 1650, and 1380 cm-
1. These bands are assigned to the O-H stretching vibration of doubly bridged hydroxyl groups (-
OHO-)39, coordinated O complexes adsorbed on Co sites40, the O-H bending vibrations in
3
adsorbed water and reaction intermediates41, and peroxide (O 2-) species11, respectively.
2
Meanwhile, new peaks were observed in the in situ Raman spectra (Fig. 5d), with the band at 526
cm-1 assigned to the O-O stretching vibration in Co-OOH42-44, and the bands at 804 and 1097 cm-
1 attributed to O 2- and O - species34, respectively, indicating the formation of new intermediates
2 2
on the catalyst surface during O decomposition. This finding is consistent with the literature
3
reports, suggesting that the peroxide intermediate is active for O catalytic decomposition.
3
Following a 24-hour exposure to an O gas flow, the Raman spectrum of 30% Co O @PCN-
3 3 4
333(Fe) showed no significant changes, which suggests that the structural integrity of the catalyst
remained intact and undamaged throughout this duration. This observation serves to confirm the
exceptional stability of the material. Furthermore, the accumulation of intermediate products was
found to be minimal, and it is noteworthy that the release of these intermediates at the active sites
constitutes the rate-limiting step in the O catalytic decomposition process, thereby providing
3
further evidence of the catalyst's outstanding performance.
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to elucidate the mechanism of O
3
decomposition over Co O @PCN-333(Fe) (Fig. 6). The model incorporates representative Fe O
3 4 3
clusters from PCN-333(Fe) and Co O nanoclusters to simulate the catalytic interface (Fig. S19).
3 4
The adsorption sites of H O and O in Co O @PCN-333(Fe) were calculated. H O was found to
2 3 3 4 2
preferentially occupy an open Fe site adjacent to the Co O , with a distance of 2.223 Å, whereas
3 4
O was located at a Co site in the vicinity of the Fe O cluster, with a distance of 1.825 Å,
3 3
highlighting the distinct roles of Fe and Co nodes in activating the two adsorbates. Subsequently,
the first O molecule preferentially adsorbs onto two adjacent open Co sites, with its two terminal
3
O atoms coordinated to them. Then, the coordinated H O at the Fe site dissociates, releasing two
2
free hydrogen atoms. One hydrogen atom reacts with the adsorbed O to generate a Co-OOOH
3
intermediate, while the other is coordinated at the interfacial O atom. The Co-OOOH species then
decomposes, releasing the first ·OOOH radical. The second O molecule subsequently adsorbs
3
onto the Co sites, during which the interfacial hydrogen-atom transfer toward the Co center and
reacts with the newly adsorbed O to form a second Co-OOOH intermediate. The decomposition
3
of this Co-OOOH intermediate releases the second ·OOOH radical, which subsequently re-adsorbs
onto Co centers to evolute the first O molecule, while leaving bridging O atoms shared by
2
neighboring Co sites. In view of the complexity of this step and its pivotal role in the overall
catalytic cycle, its kinetics were explicitly evaluated. The elementary step in which the *OOOH
intermediate forms the first O molecule and *OH (TS1), as well as the subsequent transfer of the
2
resulting *OH (TS2), was calculated. According to the DFT results, the Gibbs free energy barrier
(TS1) for the formation of *O and *OH intermediates from *OOOH is 0.47 eV, and the barrier
2
for the transfer of the generated *OH to the O atom of Fe-O-Co (TS2) is 0.64 eV. These DFT-
calculated energy barriers are moderate, indicating that the reaction process is kinetically feasible.
Finally, the transient Co-OOH intermediate decomposes to release the third O molecule, after
2
which both hydrogen atoms return to the Fe site to reconstitute the coordinated water. Overall, the
key driving force of the O catalytic decomposition process on Co O @PCN-333(Fe) is hydrogen-
3 3 4
atom transfer mechanism (Tables S3-S4 and Fig. S20), in which hydrogen atoms was transferred
among the Fe O cluster, the interfacial oxygen and the Co sites, ensuring continuous regeneration
3
of active centers. In addition, the O desorption barrier on bare Co O was also calculated and
2 3 4
found to be 1.84 eV (Fig. S21), which is much higher than the corresponding value of 0.62 eV on
Co O @PCN-333(Fe), underscoring the advantage of the hydrogen-atom transfer nanoreactor.
3 4
The above results indicated that the hydrogen-atom transfer between the interface between Co
3 4
and Fe O cluster enable stepwise O activation, efficient O release, and accelerated active-site
3 3 2
regeneration, thereby accounting for the high catalytic activity observed experimentally.

Computational details
All DFT calculations were carried out using the CP2K code (V2024.1)45. The Gaussian-and-plane-
wave (GPW) scheme was employed. Core electrons were described by norm-conserving
Goedecker–Teter–Hutter (GTH) pseudopotentials46-48, and the valence electron wavefunctions
were expanded in double-ζ Gaussian basis sets with polarization functions49, together with an
auxiliary plane-wave basis set with a kinetic energy cutoff of 450 Ry. Exchange–correlation effects
were treated within the generalized-gradient approximation using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof
(PBE) functional50. Geometry optimizations were performed with the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-

for using the DFT-D3 dispersion correction with an empirical damping function51. For Fe- and Co-

## Abstract

Ground-level ozone (O ) is a major air pollutant, and catalytic decomposition represents a
3
promising strategy for its removal. However, maintaining high catalytic efficiency under humid
conditions remains a considerable challenge. In this study, we encapsulate ultrafine metal oxides
(UMOs; e.g., Co O , NiO) within the nanopores of an Fe O-cluster-based metal–organic
3 4 3
framework, PCN-333(Fe), for catalytic O decomposition. The optimized 30% Co O @PCN-
3 3 4
333(Fe) catalyst achieves sustained 100% O conversion for over 120 hours in a continuous airflow
3
containing 40 ppm O under high space velocity (1.75 × 105 Sh-1) and a broad range of humidity
3
(10-90% RH). Mechanistic investigations reveal that the exceptional performance originates from
an interfacial hydrogen-atom transfer process between Co O and the Fe O clusters of PCN-
3 4 3
333(Fe), as confirmed by in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier-transform spectroscopy
(DRIFTS) and in situ Raman spectroscopy. This work proposes a general principle for designing
humidity-immune catalytic interfaces between metal oxides and porous materials, thereby
providing a practical foundation for sustainable control of pollutant emissions in complex
environments.

---

## Introduction

Ground-level ozone (O ) has emerged as a major global air pollutant, posing serious threats to both
3
environmental quality and public health1, 2. Outdoor O is primarily generated through
3
photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds under sunlight,
while indoor O may accumulate from emissions produced by photocopiers, laser printers,
3
ultraviolet lamps, and disinfection devices3, 4. As a potent oxidant, O remains relatively stable at
3
typical ambient concentrations (ppb level)5; however, long-term exposure has been associated with
respiratory disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and even premature mortality6, 7. The World Health
Organization has recommended that the 8-h average O concentration exceeding 100 μg m-3 (≈ 51
3
ppb) poses health risks8. Alarmingly, O levels exceeding 150 ppb are frequently reported in many
3
regions, reflecting severe pollution episodes. These observations underscore the urgent need for
efficient, durable, and environmentally sustainable strategies for O removal.
3
Among various control measures, catalytic decomposition is regarded as the most promising
strategy owing to its high efficiency and absence of harmful by-products9, 10. Conventional
transition-metal oxides exhibit notable activity but suffer from rapid deactivation under humid
conditions, where water molecules compete strongly for active sites11-13. Dispersing ultrafine metal
oxides (UMOs) on carbonaceous or porous substrates can partially alleviate these issues14, yet such
systems still face challenges of weak host–guest interfacial coupling, limited control over particle
size, and heterogeneous distributions of active sites. In contrast, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)
offer distinct advantages, including tunable organic linkers to balance
hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, robust inorganic nodes to act as active sites, and hierarchical
porosity to facilitate mass transport15-19. Nevertheless, most reported UMO-MOF composites rely
on external loading, which often leads to non-uniform particle distributions, pore blockage, and
reduced accessibility of active sites20-22. Therefore, designing UMO-MOF catalysts with well-
defined structures, strong interfacial interactions, and high stability is of paramount importance,
offering new opportunities to overcome current limitations and realize highly efficient O
3
catalytic
decomposition.
Herein, we report a series of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) composites (UMOs = ultrafine Co O or
3 4
NiO nanoparticles), in which the oxide nanoparticles are precisely encapsulated inside the
nanopores of PCN-333(Fe) rather than simply deposited on the external surface. Among them, 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) achieves 100% O conversion across a wide humidity (10-90% RH) at room
3 4 3
temperature, and maintains long-term stability for over 120 h. DFT calculations combined with in
situ spectroscopy reveal that the exceptional catalytic performance originates from interfacial
hydrogen-atom transfer between Co O and Fe O clusters of PCN-333(Fe), which facilitates
3 4 3
stepwise O activation, improves O release efficiency, and accelerates active-site regeneration.
3 2
Furthermore, the remarkable humidity immunity arises from the MOF-confined protection of
active sites from water invasion, while water molecules actively participate in the reaction pathway
rather than competing with O . This work establishes a fundamental principle for engineering
3

practical foundation for achieving sustainable pollutant control under complex and variable
environmental conditions.

---

## Results

Syntheses and Structural Characterization of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe)
The synthetic route of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) is depicted in Fig. 1. A sonication-microwave
confinement strategy was developed to achieve the precise incorporation of ultrafine metal oxide
nanoparticles within the nanopores of PCN-333(Fe). Initially, activated PCN-333(Fe) was
dispersed homogeneously in a hydrophobic solvent (e.g. n-hexane) by ultrasonication, preventing
aggregation and exposing the hierarchical pore system. Subsequently, controlled amounts of
UMOs precursors were introduced under 0°C, enabling their gradual penetration into the
nanopores of framework. After an aging process that facilitated precursor anchoring, the mixture
was carefully filtered and underwent microwave treatment, which induced rapid in situ nucleation
and growth of UMOs as highly dispersed clusters confined within the pores of PCN-333(Fe). This
step ensured both uniform nanoparticle distribution and preservation of the host crystallinity.
Finally, careful purification removed residual reactants without damaging the porous architecture.
This synthetic strategy thus provides a versatile platform for embedding nanoscale metal oxides
into MOFs, achieving strong interfacial coupling and well-defined hybrid architectures for
catalytic applications.
To elucidate the structural characteristics of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe), we selected 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) as a representative material. The MTN-type zeolitic topology of PCN-333
3 4
(Fig. 1) consists of a dual-mesopore network formed by supertetrahedral building units, with two
types of mesocages (4.2 and 5.5 nm in diameter) interconnected by pore windows of ∼2.6 and 3.0
nm, thereby providing spatially well-defined compartments for nanoparticle encapsulation23, 24.
Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy
(AC-HAADF-STEM) was employed to probe the structural integrity and encapsulation behavior25.
The pristine PCN-333(Fe) framework displays periodically arranged mesopores on the (110) plane
(Fig. 2a). Upon encapsulation, the 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe) sample preserves the parent pore
3 4
periodicity (Fig. 2b), yet exhibits locally elevated contrast, directly evidencing pore occupation by
Co O nanoparticles (Fig. 2c). EDS elemental mapping further confirms homogeneous Co
3 4
distribution across single MOF crystals (Fig. S1). The encapsulated Co O nanoparticles exhibit a
3 4
uniform size of 3.4-3.9 nm (average 3.6 ± 0.1 nm, Fig. S2), which matches the mesoporous cavity
dimensions of PCN-333. Scanning Electron Microscope reveals well-retained octahedral
morphology with smooth surfaces and absence of surface-deposited aggregates (Fig. S3),
corroborating true intracrystalline encapsulation. These observations unambiguously confirm that
Co O nanoparticles are formed in situ and precisely confined within the nanopores of PCN-
3 4
333(Fe), without compromising the structural integrity of its framework.
To probe the chemical state of Co element in 30% Co O @PCN-333(Fe), Co K-edge X-ray
3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4

3 4
identity as Co O 31, 32. N adsorption isotherms (Fig. 3f) and pore size analysis (Fig. S6) reveal a
3 4 2

3 4

333(Fe), as confirmed by in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier-transform spectroscopy

## Introduction

Ground-level ozone (O ) has emerged as a major global air pollutant, posing serious threats to both
3
environmental quality and public health1, 2. Outdoor O is primarily generated through
3
photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds under sunlight,
while indoor O may accumulate from emissions produced by photocopiers, laser printers,
3
ultraviolet lamps, and disinfection devices3, 4. As a potent oxidant, O remains relatively stable at
3
typical ambient concentrations (ppb level)5; however, long-term exposure has been associated with
respiratory disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and even premature mortality6, 7. The World Health
Organization has recommended that the 8-h average O concentration exceeding 100 μg m-3 (≈ 51
3
ppb) poses health risks8. Alarmingly, O levels exceeding 150 ppb are frequently reported in many
3
regions, reflecting severe pollution episodes. These observations underscore the urgent need for
efficient, durable, and environmentally sustainable strategies for O removal.
3
Among various control measures, catalytic decomposition is regarded as the most promising
strategy owing to its high efficiency and absence of harmful by-products9, 10. Conventional
transition-metal oxides exhibit notable activity but suffer from rapid deactivation under humid
conditions, where water molecules compete strongly for active sites11-13. Dispersing ultrafine metal
oxides (UMOs) on carbonaceous or porous substrates can partially alleviate these issues14, yet such
systems still face challenges of weak host–guest interfacial coupling, limited control over particle
size, and heterogeneous distributions of active sites. In contrast, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)
offer distinct advantages, including tunable organic linkers to balance
hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, robust inorganic nodes to act as active sites, and hierarchical
porosity to facilitate mass transport15-19. Nevertheless, most reported UMO-MOF composites rely
on external loading, which often leads to non-uniform particle distributions, pore blockage, and
reduced accessibility of active sites20-22. Therefore, designing UMO-MOF catalysts with well-
defined structures, strong interfacial interactions, and high stability is of paramount importance,
offering new opportunities to overcome current limitations and realize highly efficient O
3
catalytic
decomposition.
Herein, we report a series of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) composites (UMOs = ultrafine Co O or
3 4
NiO nanoparticles), in which the oxide nanoparticles are precisely encapsulated inside the
nanopores of PCN-333(Fe) rather than simply deposited on the external surface. Among them, 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) achieves 100% O conversion across a wide humidity (10-90% RH) at room
3 4 3
temperature, and maintains long-term stability for over 120 h. DFT calculations combined with in
situ spectroscopy reveal that the exceptional catalytic performance originates from interfacial
hydrogen-atom transfer between Co O and Fe O clusters of PCN-333(Fe), which facilitates
3 4 3
stepwise O activation, improves O release efficiency, and accelerates active-site regeneration.
3 2
Furthermore, the remarkable humidity immunity arises from the MOF-confined protection of
active sites from water invasion, while water molecules actively participate in the reaction pathway
rather than competing with O . This work establishes a fundamental principle for engineering
3
interfacial hydrogen-atom transfer within MOF-confined oxide catalysts, thereby providing a
practical foundation for achieving sustainable pollutant control under complex and variable
environmental conditions.

---

## Results

Syntheses and Structural Characterization of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe)
The synthetic route of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe) is depicted in Fig. 1. A sonication-microwave
confinement strategy was developed to achieve the precise incorporation of ultrafine metal oxide
nanoparticles within the nanopores of PCN-333(Fe). Initially, activated PCN-333(Fe) was
dispersed homogeneously in a hydrophobic solvent (e.g. n-hexane) by ultrasonication, preventing
aggregation and exposing the hierarchical pore system. Subsequently, controlled amounts of
UMOs precursors were introduced under 0°C, enabling their gradual penetration into the
nanopores of framework. After an aging process that facilitated precursor anchoring, the mixture
was carefully filtered and underwent microwave treatment, which induced rapid in situ nucleation
and growth of UMOs as highly dispersed clusters confined within the pores of PCN-333(Fe). This
step ensured both uniform nanoparticle distribution and preservation of the host crystallinity.
Finally, careful purification removed residual reactants without damaging the porous architecture.
This synthetic strategy thus provides a versatile platform for embedding nanoscale metal oxides
into MOFs, achieving strong interfacial coupling and well-defined hybrid architectures for
catalytic applications.
To elucidate the structural characteristics of UMOs@PCN-333(Fe), we selected 30%
Co O @PCN-333(Fe) as a representative material. The MTN-type zeolitic topology of PCN-333
3 4
(Fig. 1) consists of a dual-mesopore network formed by supertetrahedral building units, with two
types of mesocages (4.2 and 5.5 nm in diameter) interconnected by pore windows of ∼2.6 and 3.0
nm, thereby providing spatially well-defined compartments for nanoparticle encapsulation23, 24.

## Introduction

Ground-level ozone (O ) has emerged as a major global air pollutant, posing serious threats to both
3
environmental quality and public health1, 2. Outdoor O is primarily generated through
3
photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds under sunlight,
while indoor O may accumulate from emissions produced by photocopiers, laser printers,
3
ultraviolet lamps, and disinfection devices3, 4. As a potent oxidant, O remains relatively stable at
3
typical ambient concentrations (ppb level)5; however, long-term exposure has been associated with
respiratory disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and even premature mortality6, 7. The World Health
Organization has recommended that the 8-h average O concentration exceeding 100 μg m-3 (≈ 51
3
ppb) poses health risks8. Alarmingly, O levels exceeding 150 ppb are frequently reported in many
3
regions, reflecting severe pollution episodes. These observations underscore the urgent need for
efficient, durable, and environmentally sustainable strategies for O removal.
3
Among various control measures, catalytic decomposition is regarded as the most promising
strategy owing to its high efficiency and absence of harmful by-products9, 10. Conventional
transition-metal oxides exhibit notable activity but suffer from rapid deactivation under humid
conditions, where water molecules compete strongly for active sites11-13. Dispersing ultrafine metal
oxides (UMOs) on carbonaceous or porous substrates can partially alleviate these issues14, yet such
systems still face challenges of weak host–guest interfacial coupling, limited control over particle
size, and heterogeneous distributions of active sites. In contrast, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)
offer distinct advantages, including tunable organic linkers to balance
hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, robust inorganic nodes to act as active sites, and hierarchical
porosity to facilitate mass transport15-19. Nevertheless, most reported UMO-MOF composites rely
on external loading, which often leads to non-uniform particle distributions, pore blockage, and
reduced accessibility of active sites20-22. Therefore, designing UMO-MOF catalysts with well-
defined structures, strong interfacial interactions, and high stability is of paramount importance,
offering new opportunities to overcome current limitations and realize highly efficient O
3
catalytic
decomposition.

3 4
NiO nanoparticles), in which the oxide nanoparticles are precisely encapsulated inside the
nanopores of PCN-333(Fe) rather than simply deposited on the external surface. Among them, 30%

3 4 3

hydrogen-atom transfer between Co O and Fe O clusters of PCN-333(Fe), which facilitates

aggregation and exposing the hierarchical pore system. Subsequently, controlled amounts of
UMOs precursors were introduced under 0°C, enabling their gradual penetration into the
nanopores of framework. After an aging process that facilitated precursor anchoring, the mixture

and growth of UMOs as highly dispersed clusters confined within the pores of PCN-333(Fe). This
step ensured both uniform nanoparticle distribution and preservation of the host crystallinity.
Finally, careful purification removed residual reactants without damaging the porous architecture.

Reply: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. As you pointed out,

analysis of spin states along the reaction pathway, we fully acknowledge its
importance for radical-involving processes. However, a rigorous, quantitative

alternative spin configurations for each intermediate and transition state, which is
beyond the scope and computational budget of the present study. In this work, all
